To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the inability of insulin to augment capillary blood volume reduces glucose uptake in obesity-related insulin resistance (IR) and that abnormalities in endothelium-derived vasodilating pathways are temporally linked to the development of IR.
endothelial-derived vasorelaxation pathways are temporally linked with the development of obesity-related IR and the ability of insulin to increase CBV.
endothelial-derived vasomotor factors are temporally linked with the development of insulin resistance and the inability of insulin to augment muscle capillary blood flow.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying the mechanisms that contribute to the development of obesity-related IR in non-human primates.
the role of endothelial dysfunction and the inability to increase capillary density in the development of obesity-related insulin resistance.
understanding the mechanisms underlying the development of IR in obesity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
temporal changes in the endothelial-derived vasodepressor system are temporally associated to the development and progression of IR.
the inability to sustain a compensatory vascular response limits the capacity to augment glucose utilization in obesity-related IR.
endothelial dysfunction precedes and is associated with the onset of obesity-related IR and the development of a blunted CBV response.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the inability of insulin to augment CBV in insulin resistance is temporally associated with a decrease in the bioavailability of endothelial-derived vasculature vasodilators.

the inability of insulin to stimulate skeletal muscle capillary growth is temporally associated with a decrease in nitric oxide bioavailability and an increase in endothelial-derived contracting factors.

endothelial dysfunction is an early and important factor in the development of IR in obesity and that the inability to sustain a compensatory response in the vasculature may limit glucose-mediated increases in skeletal muscle CBV and glucose uptake.
The main takeaway from our work is that

endothelial dysfunction is a key factor in the development of insulin resistance, and that the development of insulin-resistance in humans may be prevented by improving endothelial function, such as through the use of exercise or drugs.

the development of insulin resistance is a dynamic process that is associated with temporal changes in endothelial-derived mediators that regulate capillary blood volume in skeletal muscle, which may represent an adaptive response to the development of insulin-resistant states.
the inability of insulin to induce an increase in skeletal muscle capillary recruitment is temporally associated with a progressive decrease in endothelial-derived nitric oxide bioavailability.
